opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the more frustrating dynamics in machine learning research. Academia rewards novelty. If you want a paper accepted at a top conference, you usually need a new method, ideally one with some conceptual cleverness, that beats the existing state of the art on some benchmark. A paper saying "we tried the simple thing, tuned it properly, and it works about as well as everything else" is much harder to get published, even though it's often the more useful finding.

That creates a few pressures. First, there's a push toward complexity, because a complex method looks like more of a contribution. Reviewers see lots of moving parts and think "this is substantial work." Second, and more insidiously, there's an incentive not to try very hard on the baselines. When you're developing your own method, you spend weeks or months tuning hyperparameters and fixing bugs, because you really want it to work. The baseline you're comparing against might get a single run with default settings from some other paper. Nobody has to be acting in bad faith for this to happen. It's just where the effort naturally goes. But the result is a systematic bias where new methods look better than they actually are.

You see this play out when someone comes along later and carefully re-implements the older, simpler approaches, and the gap shrinks or disappears entirely. There have been a bunch of these "reality check" papers in different subfields, and they tend to be sobering reading.

For safety research in particular, I think this matters a lot. What we want is to know which techniques actually work and why, so we can rely on them when the stakes are high. If the literature is full of complicated methods whose advantages are partly artifacts of weak comparisons, that's actively misleading. It can send people down paths that don't pan out.

So my general advice, both for myself and for people I work with, is to really respect simple baselines. Try the dumbest thing that could possibly work first, and put real effort into making it work. If your fancy method still wins after that, great, you've learned something real. And if it doesn't, that's also valuable, even if it's harder to turn into a paper. Industry labs are somewhat better placed here, since the goal is more often "does this actually work?" than "is this publishable?", but they aren't immune either. Everyone likes having a clever idea.

r001.rationale: The response says baselines often receive less tuning effort and may use default settings, but it does not say academia rewards this because poorly tuned baselines are difficult to detect.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the places where the incentives in academia are pretty clearly misaligned with what we'd actually want, which is just finding out what's true.

The basic dynamic is: you get a paper accepted by showing that your method beats the baselines. And the thing is, there's nobody whose job it is to make the baselines good. The person running the experiment is the person who proposed the new method, and they are, understandably, going to spend most of their time tuning their own method, because that's the thing they care about, and the thing they understand. The baseline gets whatever hyperparameters were in the original paper, or whatever was lying around in the codebase, and then it underperforms, and your method wins.

And I don't even think this is mostly malicious. It's more that tuning is this really tedious, thankless activity, and you only do as much of it as you have to. If you tune your baseline well and it turns out to match your method, you've just spent a lot of compute to kill your own paper. So the incentive gradient points very strongly in one direction.

Then there's a second thing, which is that complexity is sort of rewarded for its own sake. If you have a simple idea, reviewers will often say it's "not novel enough" or "too incremental," even if it works really well. Whereas if you have this elaborate method with four components and a new loss term, it looks like a contribution. So you get this pressure to add machinery, and then you have papers where, if you did the ablations carefully, you'd find that one of the four components is doing all the work, and often that component is basically "we tuned the learning rate."

My favorite example of this is in deep RL, where a bunch of papers came out claiming improvements over, say, DQN or PPO, and then people went back and found that a lot of the gains disappeared when you actually gave the baselines the same hyperparameter search budget. And there was that work showing that different random seeds alone could produce differences as large as the ones being reported as improvements. Which is pretty damning, because it means a lot of the field's "results" were, to some extent, noise plus under-tuned baselines.

Now, I do want to be fair. I think things have gotten somewhat better. Reviewers ask for ablations more, there's more awareness of the seed-variance issue, and there are now benchmark papers and reproducibility efforts whose whole point is to do the boring tuning work properly. And honestly, the shift towards large-scale models has changed the dynamic a bit, because when experiments cost a lot, people become more careful about what they run, and simple methods that scale tend to win out over clever methods that don't.

But the underlying structural problem is still there: the person evaluating the idea is the person who proposed it, and the reward is for the idea winning, not for the evaluation being right. Until you fix that, you'll keep getting this pattern, and I think the right response, as a reader, is to have a pretty strong prior that a reported improvement from a new complex method is smaller than it looks, and to weight things much more heavily when they've been replicated by someone who had no stake in the outcome.

r001.rationale: The response attributes poorly tuned baselines to misaligned incentives, lack of responsibility for tuning, and researchers favoring their own methods. It does not say academia rewards them because they are difficult to detect.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a pretty clear incentive to produce something novel, and that often means producing a more complicated method. If you take an existing method and tune it really carefully, and it turns out to work just as well as the fancy new method, that’s useful information. But it’s much harder to get a paper out of it.

You don’t need anyone to be deliberately misleading for this to cause problems. You spend a lot of time developing your method, so you understand its quirks and how to make it work. Then you compare it to a baseline using some fairly standard settings. Your method wins, but some of that difference may just be the effort you put into getting it to work.

What we’d really like to know is whether the new idea adds value given comparable effort on both sides. And the incentives don’t reliably reward finding that out, especially when the answer is that the simpler thing works just as well.

r001.rationale: The response describes incentives for novelty and unequal effort spent tuning methods and baselines, but it does not say that poorly tuned baselines are rewarded because their poor tuning is difficult to detect.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real incentive problem here. If you come up with a complicated new method and it beats the baseline, that’s a publishable result. If you spend the same amount of time tuning the baseline and discover that it does just as well, that can be a much harder paper to publish, even though you may have learned something equally useful.

And this doesn’t require anyone to be dishonest. When you’re developing your method, you naturally spend a lot of time understanding it, figuring out which hyperparameters work, and choosing settings where it performs well. You probably don’t have the same expertise with every baseline. So you can end up with a comparison that looks convincing but is partly measuring how much effort went into each side.

What I’d like is for us to reward work that tells us what actually matters. Sometimes that’s a new algorithm. Sometimes it’s showing that a simple approach works surprisingly well when you get the details right. The latter can save everyone a lot of effort, but our incentives don’t consistently reflect that.

r001.rationale: The response describes publication incentives and unequal effort or expertise in tuning methods and baselines, but does not say that poorly tuned baselines are rewarded because their poor tuning is difficult to detect.
